That PR makes an interrupted batched bootstrap resumable from its `refs/gitsync/bootstrap/*` marker under replicate, but two shapes remain outside the resume route — both surfaced and confirmed by the PR's code review.

## 1. Partial-progress resume (the sharpened remainder of the original wedge)

`replicateBootstrapRoute` requires **all** desired target refs to be absent, because `BuildBootstrapPlans` refuses targets whose desired refs exist. A multi-branch bootstrap interrupted **after any branch finalized** (trunk done, secondary branch mid-flight) therefore can never resume batching: the remaining branch goes as one unsubdividable replicate pack. The live marker is preserved and anchors the delta (PR #116's prune guard), so the pack shrinks relative to a fresh transfer — but if the residual delta exceeds the target's pack cap, the repo wedges exactly like <issue id="ca35a5b4-c595-4ffd-bf20-b7c1fd3dd331" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-2054/interrupted-batched-bootstrap-can-never-resume-the-resume-ref">ENT-2054</issue>.

Fix shape: subset bootstrap — when a live marker exists and *some* desired refs are absent, route only the absent subset through the bootstrap strategy (existing target refs already serve as haves via `completedRefs`). Needs decisions on mixed-run semantics: what the Result reports, that prune is skipped for the run, and that present branches stay stale until the next delivery (a dormant upstream means no next delivery — consider a follow-up kick).

## 2. Sync mode has no resume route at all

The routing lives in the replicate-only syncer method; `sync --all-refs --prune` against a marker-bearing target still disqualifies bootstrap via `planner.CanBootstrapRelay` (prune disables it outright, `relay.go`). Same wedge shape as the original ticket, different mode. PR #116 only fixed sync mode's destructive half (its prune no longer deletes live markers, via the shared `addPruneCandidates` exception). Wants the marker routing hoisted somewhere both modes share — likely the planner.

Related: sync mode also still labels a resume `empty-target-managed-refs` (`syncer.go:953`), so the new `relay_reason` signal never reaches `sync` — the routing hoist should fix the label with it.

## 3. Batched cutover deletes its temp ref on a create it cannot confirm

`bootstrap.go` cutover (~`:687`) deletes the temp ref unconditionally, while the branch create rides the preceding best-effort push. Under `BestEffort` the pusher swallows a per-ref `ng` and returns nil (`gitproto/push.go`, `OnRejection`), so a rejected create still reaches the delete — destroying the resume position for a branch that was never created.

**Pre-existing, not a regression:** the same probe fails identically on `origin/main`. PR #116 fixed exactly this hazard on the one-shot path (by dropping strategy-side cleanup and deferring to prune, which classifies a live marker correctly); the batched path wants the same treatment, or a rejection-aware signal plumbed into the strategy. Reachable from the CLI, where `--all-refs` implies best-effort for both `bootstrap` and `sync`.

Your pass 3 verdict 4 called the best-effort cleanup "correct" on the strength of my comment claiming every ref had landed; that claim was the false premise.

content.text: An interrupted batched bootstrap leaves behind a resume marker that, being an unexpected extra ref on the target, disqualified the bootstrap strategy on every later sync — so the repo fell back to unbatched replicate forever and could never finish importing; the fix makes that marker *select* bootstrap instead, which resumes from the exact checkpoint it records.

message.content: what does the git-sync marker record?

attachment.turnReminder: Be concise: lead with the result, skip preamble and narration, keep only what the user needs.

content.text:
One ref per branch, and its whole payload is a single commit hash: `refs/gitsync/bootstrap/heads/<branch>` → the tip of the last checkpoint whose pack the target actually accepted. The name says which branch, the value says how far that branch got.

Nothing else is persisted — the commit chain, checkpoint placement, and batch sizing are all re-derived from the source on the next run. That's why resume tolerates a changed `--target-max-pack-bytes` between attempts: `BootstrapResumeIndex` looks for the marker's hash in the newly planned checkpoint list, and failing that `chainPosition` finds it in the first-parent/topo chain and re-plans the remainder from there. If the hash isn't in the chain at all (history rewritten upstream), the marker is deleted and the bootstrap starts fresh.

Two consequences worth knowing: progress is per-branch (a multi-branch bootstrap has one marker each, which is why partial progress is the ENT-2060 gap), and the hash doubles as a fetch *have* — the source only sends objects past that point, which is what makes a resumed run incremental rather than a re-download.

Brings ENT-2054's git-sync fix into the worker, plus the observability that should have made ENT-2054 a log query instead of a code read.

## What's here

**`532e872` — bump git-sync to `988d9f2`** (`v0.9.1-0.20260831085214-988d9f2730b5`, from [git-sync#116](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/116)). An interrupted batched bootstrap leaves a `refs/gitsync/bootstrap/*` resume marker on the target; under this worker's `replicate --all-refs --prune` shape that marker was just an undesired target ref, so it disqualified the bootstrap strategy on every later sync and the repo was routed to unbatched replicate forever. The artifact of the only strategy that could resume was what locked that strategy out. git-sync now routes on the marker and resumes from the checkpoint it records.

**`9b2fed3` — log the routing decision.** `operation_mode`, `transfer_mode`, `relay_reason` on "Sync complete". The worker recorded that a sync ran but never which strategy git-sync chose, which is precisely why ENT-2054 took a source read to diagnose rather than a query. A repo stuck on the wrong route is now one query away.

## Why this matters now

This is the half that heals the stranded repos. `gh/nicschick/vc3r` (`01KXK4WZWXD1PEP16K9V6CMFHA`, eu-central-1) has been wedged since 2026-07-15 behind a bootstrap marker with no `refs/heads/main`; `gh/nicschick/rci` (`01KXK4WZS7M270NSABM94DRF01`) is the same shape but latent — no sync jobs at all, so it takes the wedged path the moment a push arrives. Neither recovers until this deploys.

## Behavior change worth knowing

git-sync no longer mirrors `refs/gitsync/*` **from** a source under `--all-refs`. This worker is a caller with entiredb-kind sources, so it's the one that can see it: on a chained mirror (A → B → C) where B holds leftover bootstrap scaffolding, that namespace stops replicating to C. # Datadog Logs

One-line summary: Search raw log entries/patterns and run SQL analytics on log data.

---

## Tools


### search_datadog_logs

Search and retrieve raw log entries or log patterns using a **concrete Datadog query**.

**Routing — call the right tool first:**
- **Natural-language or diagnostic questions** ("any errors in X?", "why is Y failing?", "anything weird with Z?") → load `datadog/semantic-search-logs` and call `semantic_search_datadog_logs` first. It maps user intent to known log-template identifiers and returns a `query_string` you can pass back into this tool. Keyword search alone usually misses the relevant logs because their messages don't contain the user's words.
- **Counting, aggregations, or numerical analysis** → MUST load `datadog/ddsql` skill first, then use `analyze_datadog_logs`.
- **Concrete facets/strings already supplied by the user** (`service:payment`, `@http.status_code:500`, a literal error message) → use this tool directly.

Best for:
1. Viewing small numbers of raw logs
2. Discovering patterns in large volumes of logs (`use_log_patterns: true`). Can discover patterns by clustering logs with similar values based on `clustering_pattern_field` parameter.
3. Discovering available custom attributes via `extra_fields` (e.g., `extra_fields: ['*']` or `extra_fields: ['http*']`), which can then be used as `extra_columns` in `analyze_datadog_logs`

| Parameter | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `query` | Yes | Datadog log search query (see syntax below) |
| `from` | No | Start time. Default: `now-1h` |
| `to` | No | End time. Default: `now` |
| `use_log_patterns` | No | Group similar logs into patterns. Default: false |
| `indexes` | No | Log indexes to search. Default: all |
| `storage_tier` | No | `indexes` (hot, default), `online-archives`, or `flex` |
| `sort` | No | Sort order. Default: `-timestamp` (newest first) |
| `start_at` | No | Offset for pagination |
| `max_tokens` | No | Max response tokens. Default: 10000 |
| `extra_fields` | No | Additional attributes/tags to include. Use **bare names without `@` or `custom.` prefix** (e.g., `duration`, not `@duration` or `custom.duration`) — the tool automatically tries all bucket prefixes. Supports wildcards (`'http*'`, `'*'` for all). |
| `clustering_pattern_field` | No | Log field used for clustering logs with similar values when use_log_patterns is true. Can cluster on any attribute or tag present in the logs. Consider '@error.message', '@errorMessage', '@error' or '@error.stack' when investigating error logs. Default: 'message' |
| `pattern_group_by` | No | Only used when `use_log_patterns: true`. List of fields/tags to split patterns by. Can group by any attribute or tag present in the logs. Suggested: `['service']`, `['source']`, or `['service', 'source']`; combine with `env` (e.g. `['service', 'env']`) to compare across environments. Each returned pattern is scoped to a unique combination of these fields, and their values appear in the `groups` column. Default: no grouping (patterns aggregate across all values) |

#### Response shape (with `extra_fields` set)

Each log entry is rendered as YAML with three sections. Knowing which section a key came from tells you how to use it in a filter or in `analyze_datadog_logs` `extra_columns`.

1. **Top-level fields** — `env`, `host`, `service`, `source`, `status`, `message`, `timestamp`, etc. Filter as bare: `env:prod`, `service:api`.
2. **`attributes:` map** — keys appear with a display prefix (`custom.X`, `error.X`). The prefix is part of how the response is displayed, not the name to use in queries.
3. **`tags:` list** of `key:value` strings. Filter as bare `key:value`.

**Critical: `extra_fields` names, response keys, and `extra_columns` names are all different — do not copy between them.**

| What you see in the response | `search_datadog_logs` `extra_fields` to request it | `analyze_datadog_logs` `extra_columns` |
|---|---|---|
| Top-level `env`, `host`, `service`, `version`, `status` | (always included) | already default columns — do not redeclare |
| `attributes: custom.duration: 42` | `duration` (bare, no prefix) | `{name: "@duration", type: "bigint"}` |
| `attributes: error.message: boom` | `error.message` | `{name: "@error.message", type: "varchar"}` |
| `tags: - image_tag:123` | `image_tag:*` (any value) or `image_tag:123` (exact) | `{name: "image_tag", type: "varchar"}` |

**`extra_fields`**: always use bare names — `duration`, not `@duration` or `custom.duration`. The tool matches the bare name against all attribute forms automatically.

**`extra_columns`**: the display prefix in the response (`custom.`, `error.`) tells you the translation rule:
- `custom.X` in response → `@X` in `extra_columns` (strip `custom.`, add `@`)
- `error.X` in response → `@error.X` in `extra_columns` (keep `error.`, add `@`)
- `tags:` entry → bare name in `extra_columns` (no `@`)

**Do not copy the response key directly into `extra_columns`.** When the response shows `custom.duration`, the `extra_columns` name is `@duration` — not `custom.duration`. Passing `custom.duration` as an `extra_columns` name produces a column that cannot be resolved, returning empty results or a 400 error.

Each `extra_columns` entry MUST be an object with both `name` and `type` fields. A bare-string array (`extra_columns: ["@http.status_code"]`) is rejected with *"extra_columns must be an array of column objects"*. Supported types: `varchar`, `bigint`, `decimal`, `boolean`, `timestamp`, `array<varchar>`, `array<bigint>`, `array<decimal>`, `array<boolean>`, `array<timestamp>` — the canonical names from `advanced_query.ExtraColumnAllowedTypes`. An unsupported type fails with *"invalid extra column type ... Supported types: ..."*.

### analyze_datadog_logs

Do NOT call analyze_datadog_logs without first calling load_datadog_skill(datadog/ddsql) in the same round-trip. Loading datadog/logs alone is not sufficient for DDSQL queries — call both skills together whenever aggregation/counting is needed. Run DDSQL (PostgreSQL-compatible) queries against a virtual `logs` table. Use for counting, aggregations, grouping, and numerical analysis.

| Parameter | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `sql_query` | Yes | DDSQL query against the `logs` table |
| `filter` | No | Pre-filter in Datadog query syntax |
| `from` | No | Start time. Default: `now-1h` |
| `to` | No | End time. Default: `now` |
| `indexes` | No | Log indexes to search |
| `storage_tier` | No | Storage tier to query |
| `start_at` | No | Offset for pagination |
| `max_tokens` | No | Max response tokens. Default: 10000 |
| `extra_columns` | No | Custom attributes as SQL columns; see "Response shape" section in `search_datadog_logs` for translation |

**Standard virtual table columns** (the ONLY columns available without `extra_columns`): `timestamp`, `host`, `service`, `env`, `version`, `status`, `message`

**IMPORTANT**: Any tag, attribute, or value referenced in the query — in `SELECT`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `ORDER BY`, or anywhere else — that is not one of the standard columns above MUST be declared in `extra_columns`. This includes:
- Custom attributes with `@` prefix (e.g., `@http.status_code`, `@duration`, `@error.message`)
- Tag keys not in the standard set (e.g., `team`, `region`, `pod_name`, `kube_namespace`)

Without `extra_columns`, the query will fail or return null for those references. Examples:

```
# SELECT @http.status_code, COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY @http.status_code
extra_columns: [{name: "@http.status_code", type: "bigint"}]

# SELECT team, region, AVG(@duration) FROM logs WHERE region = 'us-east-1' GROUP BY team, region
extra_columns: [{name: "team", type: "varchar"}, {name: "region", type: "varchar"}, {name: "@duration", type: "bigint"}]
```

Use `search_datadog_logs` with `extra_fields: ['*']` first to discover which custom attributes/tags exist on the logs you care about, then pass those names into `extra_columns`. See the **Response shape** section above for the full translation from response keys to `extra_columns` declarations.

**Rule of thumb — `extra_columns`:** **bare name → tag**, **`@` prefix → attribute**. In `sql_query`, reference each column by the exact name declared in `extra_columns` (quote names that contain `@` or `.`). Do **not** use `tags->team` or `tags['team']` — these are not valid column accessors.

**Do not use `custom.X` or `attributes.X` as `extra_columns` names or in `sql_query`.** If `search_datadog_logs` showed `custom.duration` in the response, the `extra_columns` name is `@duration`. Declaring `{name: "custom.duration"}` causes the generated SQL to contain `"custom.duration"` as a column name, which cannot be resolved — you will get empty results or a 400 error. The display prefix in the search response is a translation hint, not the column name.

```sql
-- ✓ Correct: attribute discovered as custom.duration in search response
-- extra_columns: [{name: "@duration", type: "bigint"}]
SELECT "@duration", COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY "@duration"

-- ✗ Wrong: copied the response key directly — custom.duration cannot be resolved
-- extra_columns: [{name: "custom.duration", type: "bigint"}]
SELECT "custom.duration", COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY "custom.duration"

-- ✓ Correct: tag by bare name, attribute with @
-- extra_columns: [{name: "team", type: "varchar"}, {name: "@http.status_code", type: "bigint"}]
SELECT team, "@http.status_code", COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY team, "@http.status_code"

-- ✗ Wrong: tags-> is not a valid column accessor
SELECT tags->team, COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY tags->team
```

**Time bucketing**: Use `DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamp)`; `TIMESTAMP_BUCKET(timestamp, '1h')` is not currently accepted by `analyze_datadog_logs`.

---

## Query Syntax

### Tags vs Attributes
- **Tags**: Direct format `key:value` — `env:prod`, `service:api`, `host:web-1`
- **Attributes**: Use `@` prefix — `@http.status_code:500`, `@user.id:123`, `@error.message:"timeout"`

### Examples
```
# Error logs from production API service
service:api env:prod status:error

# 4xx or 5xx HTTP errors
@http.status_code:[400 TO 599]

# Database queries taking over 1 second
service:database @duration:>1000

# Specific user's session
@user.id:abc123

# All logs except health checks
service:api -@url:/health

# Multiple services with errors
(service:api OR service:worker) AND status:error

# URL pattern matching
@http.url:/api/v*/users/*
```

### SQL Analysis Examples
```sql
-- Count errors by service
SELECT service, COUNT(*) as error_count
FROM logs
WHERE status = 'error'
GROUP BY service
ORDER BY error_count DESC

-- Error rate by hour
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamp) as bucket,
       COUNT(*) as total,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'error' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as errors
FROM logs
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamp)
ORDER BY bucket

-- Group by a non-standard tag and a custom attribute — both MUST be in extra_columns
-- extra_columns: [{name: "team", type: "varchar"}, {name: "@http.status_code", type: "bigint"}]
SELECT team, "@http.status_code", COUNT(*) as cnt
FROM logs
WHERE status = 'error'
GROUP BY team, "@http.status_code"
ORDER BY cnt DESC
```

## Best Practices

- Use `status:error` to find errors quickly
- Filter by `service` first to narrow scope
- Use `use_log_patterns: true` to reduce duplicate log entries in large result sets
- Combine `use_log_patterns: true` with `pattern_group_by` to get one pattern per group — `['service']` or `['source']` are the most useful starting points; add `env` or `host` to compare across environments or hosts
- Set `max_tokens` appropriately (5000-10000 for overview, 20000-50000 for details)
- Use `extra_fields` with wildcards to discover custom attributes, then use those in `analyze_datadog_logs` via `extra_columns`
- In `analyze_datadog_logs`, anything referenced in the SQL that is not one of `timestamp`, `host`, `service`, `env`, `version`, `status`, `message` (custom attributes, additional tags) MUST be passed in `extra_columns`
- For aggregations and counting, always prefer `analyze_datadog_logs` over `search_datadog_logs`


---
Related skills for this domain: datadog/querying-patterns, datadog/traces, datadog/visualizations
Load with `load_datadog_skill` for additional guidance.

extra_columns: [{name: "@http.status_code", type: "bigint"}]

# SELECT team, region, AVG(@duration) FROM logs WHERE region = 'us-east-1' GROUP BY team, region
extra_columns: [{name: "team", type: "varchar"}, {name: "region", type: "varchar"}, {name: "@duration", type: "bigint"}]
```

Use `search_datadog_logs` with `extra_fields: ['*']` first to discover which custom attributes/tags exist on the logs you care about, then pass those names into `extra_columns`. See the **Response shape** section above for the full translation from response keys to `extra_columns` declarations.

**Rule of thumb — `extra_columns`:** **bare name → tag**, **`@` prefix → attribute**. In `sql_query`, reference each column by the exact name declared in `extra_columns` (quote names that contain `@` or `.`). Do **not** use `tags->team` or `tags['team']` — these are not valid column accessors.

**Do not use `custom.X` or `attributes.X` as `extra_columns` names or in `sql_query`.** If `search_datadog_logs` showed `custom.duration` in the response, the `extra_columns` name is `@duration`. Declaring `{name: "custom.duration"}` causes the generated SQL to contain `"custom.duration"` as a column name, which cannot be resolved — you will get empty results or a 400 error. The display prefix in the search response is a translation hint, not the column name.

```sql
-- ✓ Correct: attribute discovered as custom.duration in search response
-- extra_columns: [{name: "@duration", type: "bigint"}]
SELECT "@duration", COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY "@duration"

-- ✗ Wrong: copied the response key directly — custom.duration cannot be resolved
-- extra_columns: [{name: "custom.duration", type: "bigint"}]
SELECT "custom.duration", COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY "custom.duration"

-- ✓ Correct: tag by bare name, attribute with @
-- extra_columns: [{name: "team", type: "varchar"}, {name: "@http.status_code", type: "bigint"}]
SELECT team, "@http.status_code", COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY team, "@http.status_code"

-- ✗ Wrong: tags-> is not a valid column accessor
SELECT tags->team, COUNT(*) FROM logs GROUP BY tags->team
```

**Time bucketing**: Use `DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamp)`; `TIMESTAMP_BUCKET(timestamp, '1h')` is not currently accepted by `analyze_datadog_logs`.

---

## Query Syntax

### Tags vs Attributes
- **Tags**: Direct format `key:value` — `env:prod`, `service:api`, `host:web-1`
- **Attributes**: Use `@` prefix — `@http.status_code:500`, `@user.id:123`, `@error.message:"timeout"`

### Examples
```
# Error logs from production API service
service:api env:prod status:error

# 4xx or 5xx HTTP errors
@http.status_code:[400 TO 599]

# Database queries taking over 1 second
service:database @duration:>1000

# Specific user's session
@user.id:abc123

# All logs except health checks
service:api -@url:/health

# Multiple services with errors
(service:api OR service:worker) AND status:error

# URL pattern matching
@http.url:/api/v*/users/*
```

### SQL Analysis Examples
```sql
-- Count errors by service
SELECT service, COUNT(*) as error_count
FROM logs
WHERE status = 'error'
GROUP BY service
ORDER BY error_count DESC

-- Error rate by hour
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamp) as bucket,
       COUNT(*) as total,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'error' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as errors
FROM logs
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamp)
ORDER BY bucket

-- Group by a non-standard tag and a custom attribute — both MUST be in extra_columns
-- extra_columns: [{name: "team", type: "varchar"}, {name: "@http.status_code", type: "bigint"}]
SELECT team, "@http.status_code", COUNT(*) as cnt
FROM logs
WHERE status = 'error'
GROUP BY team, "@http.status_code"
ORDER BY cnt DESC
```

## Best Practices

- Use `status:error` to find errors quickly
- Filter by `service` first to narrow scope
- Use `use_log_patterns: true` to reduce duplicate log entries in large result sets
- Combine `use_log_patterns: true` with `pattern_group_by` to get one pattern per group — `['service']` or `['source']` are the most useful starting points; add `env` or `host` to compare across environments or hosts
- Set `max_tokens` appropriately (5000-10000 for overview, 20000-50000 for details)
- Use `extra_fields` with wildcards to discover custom attributes, then use those in `analyze_datadog_logs` via `extra_columns`
- In `analyze_datadog_logs`, anything referenced in the SQL that is not one of `timestamp`, `host`, `service`, `env`, `version`, `status`, `message` (custom attributes, additional tags) MUST be passed in `extra_columns`
- For aggregations and counting, always prefer `analyze_datadog_logs` over `search_datadog_logs`


---

Load with `load_datadog_skill` for additional guidance.

Not yet — the logs say the fix isn't live, and the two repos haven't healed.

**The deploy hasn't rolled out.** 80,278 "Sync complete" lines in the last 2 days, and not one carries `relay_reason` / `transfer_mode` / `operation_mode`. They all carry `applied` and `target_ulid`, which come from the same log call — so if the new build were running, the new fields would be right there beside them. That merge is ~20 minutes old and hasn't shipped.

**`vc3r` is still wedged.** Over 30 days it logs "Processing git job" nine times (most recently 2026-08-28) and reaches "Sync complete" exactly zero times. Jobs arrive, the sync never completes — the ticket's symptom, unchanged.

**`rci` is still silent**, as expected for a dormant upstream; it'll take the resume path on its first push.

So closing now would be closing on a merge, not on a fix. What I'd want before closing:

1. Worker deploy rolls out — confirmable in one query (any `relay_reason` at all).
2. `vc3r` logs `relay_reason=bootstrap-resume-marker`, then its first-ever "Sync complete".

`rci` I wouldn't block on; it can't demonstrate anything until someone pushes to it.

Ping me once the deploy lands and I'll run both checks — it's about a minute of queries, and then closing is backed by evidence rather than optimism.

{"id":"ENT-1948","title":"Mirror sync permanently fails when catch-up pack exceeds 10 GiB receive-pack body cap","description":"## Symptom

Every sync of mirror placement `01KXK4WZWXD1PEP16K9V6CMFHA` (GitHub repo `nicschick/vc3r`, private, eu-central-1) fails with:

```
sync: replicate relay failed: replicate execute: push target refs: report-status: unpack error: push rejected: body exceeded size limit 10737418240
```

## Root cause

git-sync relays the pack fetched from GitHub as a push to the regional git endpoint (`svctok.aws-eu-central-1.entire.internal:8281/git/repo/01KXK4...`). entire-server's receive-pack rejects the request body at exactly 10 GiB (10737418240 bytes) after ~5 min of streaming. Server-side twin log at the same second: `service:entire-server "receive-pack: push rejected by size limit"` (WARN, hosts camembert/gorgonzola/roquefort, eu-central-1).

Because the target never applies the pack, the mirror never converges: every GitHub push webhook re-triggers the same doomed ~5 min / ~10 GiB transfer. Any repo whose missing delta exceeds 10 GiB is wedged forever.

## Evidence

All 7 fleet-wide size-limit rejections in the last 15 days are this single placement (UTC):

* Aug 22 17:48, 17:50
* Aug 23 12:40, 12:45, 19:29
* Aug 24 18:56
* Aug 25 14:03

Zero successful syncs in the window. On Aug 22 mirror-worker also logged `Failure-index entry evicted: failing past max age, giving up (recover via L2 if still needed)`, so it was already failing before Aug 22 (168h max age exceeded).

Datadog: mirror-worker `Permanent sync error, terminating` carries the error in `@error`; join key is `@target_ulid` (free-text search does not match these attributes).

## Impact

* One customer mirror permanently stale/empty in eu-central-1.
* ~10 GiB GitHub egress + internal transfer and ~5 min of a mirror-worker slot wasted per push to that repo.
* Failure mode is silent today: no monitor fires on it.

## Proposed fixes

1. Recover this placement via L2 seeding (as the eviction log suggests) so future deltas fit under the cap.
2. Exempt or raise the cap for internal relay pushes. The 10 GiB limit targets external pushers but permanently wedges the sync path.
3. Chunk relay pushes (batch refs so no single receive-pack body exceeds the cap). Does not help when a single ref delta is over 10 GiB.
4. If the repo is not worth mirroring, tear down the placement to stop the waste.

## Follow-up

content.text:
They overlap on one repo, but they're different bugs — and the distinction is worth keeping:

- **ENT-1948 is the wall:** entire-server's receive-pack rejects a >10 GiB body, so the relay push fails.
- **ENT-2054 is why hitting the wall is permanent:** the marker left by the interrupted attempt disqualifies the strategy that could resume, so the repo re-attempts the same doomed unbatched push forever — from *any* interruption, not just that cap.

The useful part: **ENT-2054's fix probably resolves ENT-1948 outright, without ENT-1948 needing its own fix.** Look at its error — `replicate execute: push target refs` — that's the replicate path shipping one giant pack, exactly because the marker locked out bootstrap. With routing fixed, vc3r goes to *batched* bootstrap, which caps packs at 512 MiB and subdivides further on rejection. ENT-1948's proposal #3 ("chunk relay pushes") is essentially what batched bootstrap already does; it just wasn't reachable. Proposals #1/#2/#4 (L2 reseed, raise the cap, tear down the placement) become unnecessary if that holds.

Two things that keep ENT-1948 from being a plain duplicate:

1. **The subdivision floor.** `subdivideCheckpoints` halves until every gap is one commit — a *single* commit whose delta exceeds 10 GiB still fails. Nobody has checked whether vc3r's >10 GiB spans multiple commits, so "fixed" is a hypothesis until the deploy proves it.
2. **The monitor.** Nothing alerts on `receive-pack: push rejected by size limit` today — that's ENT-1948's follow-up and my PR does nothing for it. That's the one piece of real remaining work.

My recommendation: link them rather than merge, and after the deploy verification most likely close ENT-1948 as resolved-by-ENT-2054 while keeping the monitor as its own small ticket. Both then hinge on the same check I described — `vc3r` reaching `relay_reason=bootstrap-resume-marker` and its first "Sync complete".

Want me to add the relation and trim ENT-1948's description down to what actually remains (verify + monitor + the floor question)?

1. **Leading token**: if the first whitespace-delimited token matches `^\d+[smhd]$` (e.g. `5m`, `2h`), that's the interval; the rest is the prompt.
2. **Trailing "every" clause**: otherwise, if the input ends with `every <N><unit>` or `every <N> <unit-word>` (e.g. `every 20m`, `every 5 minutes`, `every 2 hours`), extract that as the interval and strip it from the prompt. Only match when what follows "every" is a time expression — `check every PR` has no interval.
3. **No interval**: otherwise, the entire input is the prompt and you'll self-pace dynamically (see "Dynamic mode" below).

If the resulting prompt is empty, show usage `/loop [interval] <prompt>` and stop.

Examples:
- `5m /babysit-prs` → interval `5m`, prompt `/babysit-prs` (rule 1)
- `check the deploy every 20m` → interval `20m`, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 2)
- `run tests every 5 minutes` → interval `5m`, prompt `run tests` (rule 2)
- `check the deploy` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check the deploy` (rule 3)
- `check every PR` → no interval → dynamic mode, prompt `check every PR` (rule 3 — "every" not followed by time)
- `5m` → empty prompt → show usage

## Offer cloud first

Before any scheduling step, check whether EITHER is true:
- the parsed interval (rule 1 or 2) is **≥60 minutes**, or
- regardless of which rule matched, the original input uses daily phrasing ("every morning", "daily", "every day", "each night", "every weekday")

If either is true, call AskUserQuestion first:
- `question`: "This loop stops when you close this session. Set it up as a cloud schedule instead so it keeps running?"
- `header`: "Schedule"
- `options`: `[{label: "Cloud schedule (recommended)", description: "Runs in Anthropic's cloud even after you close this session"}, {label: "This session only", description: "Runs in this terminal until you exit"}]`

If they pick **Cloud schedule**: do NOT call CronCreate. Invoke the `schedule` skill directly via the Skill tool with `args` set to their original input verbatim (e.g. `Skill({skill: "schedule", args: "every morning tell me a joke"})`), then follow that skill's instructions to completion. Do NOT tell the user to run /schedule themselves. **Then stop — do not continue to any section below** (no CronCreate, no ScheduleWakeup, no "execute the prompt now").
If they pick **This session only**:
- If the trigger was a parsed ≥60-minute interval (rule 1 or 2): continue below with that interval.
- If the trigger was daily phrasing only (rule 3, no parsed interval): do NOT call CronCreate. Explain that a daily-cadence loop won't fire before this session closes, so there's nothing useful to schedule locally — suggest they either pick Cloud schedule, or re-run `/loop` with an explicit shorter interval (e.g. `/loop 1h <prompt>`) if they want a session loop. Then stop.
If neither trigger condition was met: continue below.

## Fixed-interval mode (rules 1 and 2)

Convert the interval to a cron expression:

| Interval pattern      | Cron expression     | Notes                                    |
|-----------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `Nm` where N ≤ 59   | `*/N * * * *`     | every N minutes                          |
| `Nm` where N ≥ 60   | `0 */H * * *`     | round to hours (H = N/60, must divide 24)|
| `Nh` where N ≤ 23   | `0 */N * * *`     | every N hours                            |
| `Nd`                | `0 0 */N * *`     | every N days at midnight local           |
| `Ns`                | treat as `ceil(N/60)m` | cron minimum granularity is 1 minute  |

**If the interval doesn't cleanly divide its unit** (e.g. `7m` → `*/7 * * * *` gives uneven gaps at :56→:00; `90m` → 1.5h which cron can't express), pick the nearest clean interval and tell the user what you rounded to before scheduling.

Then:
1. Call CronCreate with: `cron` (the expression above), `prompt` (the parsed prompt verbatim), `recurring: true`.
2. Briefly confirm: what's scheduled, the cron expression, the human-readable cadence, that recurring tasks auto-expire after 7 days, and that the user can cancel sooner with CronDelete (include the job ID). Only if you did NOT show the cloud-offer AskUserQuestion above (i.e., neither trigger condition applied), end the confirmation with this exact line on its own, italicized: `_Runs until you close this session · For durable cloud-based loops, use /schedule_`. If the user already answered that question, omit this line.
3. **Then immediately execute the parsed prompt now** — don't wait for the first cron fire. If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.

## Dynamic mode (rule 3 — no interval)

The user wants you to self-pace. Decide what makes the next iteration worth running — a passage of time, or an observable event.

1. **Run the parsed prompt now.** If it's a slash command, invoke it via the Skill tool; otherwise act on it directly.
2. **If the next run is gated on an event** (CI finishing, a log line matching, a file changing, a PR comment) and no Monitor is already running for it: arm one now with `persistent: true`. Its events arrive as `<task-notification>` messages and wake this loop immediately — you do not wait for the ScheduleWakeup deadline. Arm once; on later iterations call TaskList first and skip this step if a monitor is already running.
3. **Briefly confirm**: that you're self-pacing, whether a Monitor is the primary wake signal, that you ran the task now, and what fallback delay you're about to pick. Write this as text *before* calling ScheduleWakeup — the turn ends as soon as that tool returns.
4. **Then, as the last action of this turn, decide whether the loop continues.** If the task needs another iteration, call ScheduleWakeup with:
   - `delaySeconds`: with a Monitor armed this is the **fallback heartbeat** — how long to wait if no event fires (lean 1200–1800s; idle ticks more frequent than the task needs are pure overhead). Without a Monitor this is the cadence — pick based on what you observed. Read the tool's own description for cache-aware delay guidance.
   - `reason`: one short sentence on why you picked that delay.
   - `prompt`: the full original /loop input verbatim, prefixed with `/loop ` so the next firing re-enters this skill and continues the loop. For example, if the user typed `/loop check the deploy`, pass `/loop check the deploy` as the prompt.
   - `noop`: `true` if this tick changed nothing ("still waiting", "quiet hold"); `false` if it did something worth keeping. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks collapse in the terminal.
   If it doesn't need another iteration, stop instead (step 6) — re-arming is a per-turn choice, not a default.
5. **If you were woken by a `<task-notification>`** rather than this prompt: handle the event in the context of the loop task, then make the same decision. If the loop should continue, call ScheduleWakeup again with the same `prompt` and the same 1200–1800s `delaySeconds` from step 4 (the Monitor remains the wake signal; the new wakeup is only the fallback heartbeat). If the event means the work is finished, stop (step 6).
6. **To stop the loop** — the task is complete, further iterations can't make progress, or the user asked you to stop — call ScheduleWakeup with `stop: true` (no other fields) and TaskStop any Monitor you armed (use TaskList to find the task ID if it is no longer in context). Stopping is the loop's normal ending — the user can restart it anytime with /loop. Before you stop, send a one-line outcome via PushNotification — the user may be away and waiting to hear it's done. Skip this if you're stopping because the user just told you to; they're already here.

content.content:
## Fix

Three steps: wipe refs (data plane) → re-drive the sync (control plane) →
verify (here).

### 1. Wipe the refs — `entiredbctl admin reset-repo-data`

Mirror-only, cluster-wide ref delete. Leaves the repos row, DHT providers,
object storage, and URL routing intact, so the repo keeps its ULID,
registration, and grants. The server **refuses non-mirror repos** (wiping a
primary's refs would be unrecoverable).

```bash
ENTIRE_BASE_URL=https://<cluster>.entire.io \
  entiredbctl admin reset-repo-data <repo-ulid> \
  --node-url https://<node>.<cluster>.entire.io --yes
```

> **Two transport gotchas, both real:**
> - **The cluster entry host can't proxy gRPC.** Its ALB target group is
>   HTTP/2-not-gRPC and bounces `application/grpc` with **HTTP 464**. So keep
>   `ENTIRE_BASE_URL` = the *cluster* URL (that's the ops-token audience +
>   `cluster_host` core's registry knows), but pass `--node-url` pointing at a
>   *specific node* (e.g. `bishop.<cluster>.entire.io`) to route the actual
>   gRPC call around the ALB. `--node-url` is optional and transport-only.
> - **The node must run the `reset-repo-data` build.** The RPC landed in entiredb
>   PR #2397. A node on an older build answers `404 → Unimplemented`. Check
>   `https://<node>.<cluster>.entire.io/health` and confirm its `version` sha
>   includes #2397.

Auth: your logged-in context (ops-token exchange at core) or a stashed
break-glass token (`entiredbctl admin break-glass`).

### 2. Re-drive the sync — `entire-core admin mirrors resume`

`resume` clears `suspended_at` **and unconditionally re-publishes a `sync_repo`
job** (`kickResumeSync`), so it works as a plain "sync now" trigger whether or
not the mirror was suspended. Idempotent.

```bash
# break-glass gets you a super-admin context if you lack platform-admin
entire-core admin break-glass          --base-url https://<region>.auth.entire.io
entire-core admin mirrors resume <repo-ulid> --base-url https://<region>.auth.entire.io
```

`mirror_repos` lives in global CockroachDB, so a resume issued against **any**
regional core is visible everywhere and the resync kick is routed to the repo's
own region.

> The `Resumed mirror …` line only *guarantees* the un-suspension committed. The
> resync kick is **best-effort** — a publish failure is logged server-side and
> swallowed. Always confirm via step 3 rather than trusting the CLI line.

content.text:
There's a runbook for exactly this repo's failure mode — `docs/runbooks/mirror-stuck-refs-without-objects.md`, written around `vc3r`.

**The one you want now is just step 2** — a plain "sync now" trigger:

```bash
entire-core admin mirrors resume 01KXK4WZWXD1PEP16K9V6CMFHA \
  --base-url https://eu-central-1.auth.entire.io
```

`resume` unconditionally re-publishes a `sync_repo` job whether or not the mirror was suspended, and it's idempotent. `mirror_repos` is global CockroachDB, so any regional core works and the kick routes to the repo's own region — but use the EU URL anyway since that's where it lives. If you lack platform-admin, `entire-core admin break-glass --base-url https://eu-central-1.auth.entire.io` first.

**Skip step 1 of that runbook** (`entiredbctl admin reset-repo-data` to wipe refs). That step exists *because* the old code couldn't escape the wedge — wiping refs was the manual workaround to force the batched path. That's precisely what we just fixed: the marker now routes to bootstrap on its own. Running it would destroy the resume position and mask whether the fix works. If the sync fails again, the wipe is still there as a fallback.

Alternative if you'd rather not use platform-admin: `mirror-pipeline-admin failindex rekick --ulid 01KXK4WZWXD1PEP16K9V6CMFHA --live` against eu-central-1 — but it needs NATS mTLS certs, and ENT-1948 recorded a "failing past max age, giving up" eviction, so the entry may not be in the index any more. Check with `failindex get` first. The runbook recommends `mirrors resume` for both reasons.

One caveat: the resync kick is best-effort — a publish failure is logged server-side and swallowed, so don't trust the CLI line. Run it and I'll confirm from the logs whether the job actually landed and which route git-sync took.
